data.title: Junior Frontend Developer
data.fitReason: Bootcamp graduates typically cover HTML, CSS, and JavaScript fundamentals — the baseline for junior frontend roles. The to-do list app likely demonstrates basic DOM manipulation or a simple React/Vue component, which is the minimum portfolio signal employers expect at this tier. No professional experience limits the score significantly.

data.title: Junior Full-Stack Developer
data.fitReason: Many bootcamps cover both frontend and backend basics. If the to-do list app includes a simple REST API or database layer, this role becomes a stretch-viable target. Competition is fierce and most listings expect at least one internship or professional project beyond a single CRUD app.

data.title: Junior Backend Developer
data.fitReason: If the bootcamp curriculum included Node.js, Python, or similar server-side content and the to-do app has a backend component, this is achievable. However, backend-only junior roles are less common than full-stack listings, and employers typically expect demonstrated API design or database skills beyond a basic to-do app.

data.title: Apprentice Software Developer
data.fitReason: Formal apprenticeship programs at companies like Accenture, IBM, or various startups are specifically designed for non-degree candidates who have completed structured training. A bootcamp certificate is a recognized qualifier. These programs trade salary for mentorship, making them a strong fit given the critical experience gap.

data.title: Junior JavaScript Developer
data.fitReason: JavaScript is the most commonly taught bootcamp language, so there is reasonable alignment with at least one language. Specialist JavaScript junior roles exist, but they still expect more than a single to-do app. Remote JavaScript junior roles are highly competitive with hundreds of similarly qualified applicants.

data.title: Technical Support Engineer (Tier 1)
data.fitReason: Bootcamp graduates with basic coding knowledge are competitive for Tier 1 technical support at SaaS companies, where understanding APIs and reading code matters. These roles pay less than development positions but provide verified professional experience — the single most critical gap in this profile.

data.title: Junior QA / Software Test Engineer
data.fitReason: QA roles are a realistic entry point for bootcamp graduates without a degree. Basic scripting knowledge is sufficient for many manual-to-automated QA positions. Employers in this space are often more flexible on portfolio depth. The role also builds professional experience fast, addressing the most urgent gap.

data.title: No-Code / Low-Code Developer
data.fitReason: Platforms like Bubble, Webflow, or Zapier require logical thinking and basic technical literacy — both plausibly present after a bootcamp. These roles are undervalued by traditional developers, creating lower competition. A to-do list app rebuilt in a no-code tool could serve as a relevant portfolio piece for this niche.

data.title: Junior WordPress Developer
data.fitReason: WordPress development requires basic PHP awareness, HTML, and CSS — skills most bootcamps touch on. The freelance and agency market for WordPress is large and relatively accessible to entry-level candidates. However, the to-do app does not directly demonstrate WordPress capability, and competition from experienced freelancers is high.

data.title: Coding Bootcamp Teaching Assistant
data.fitReason: Many bootcamps hire recent graduates as teaching assistants or tutors to support current cohorts. The candidate has directly relevant and recent experience with the curriculum. The role builds communication, mentorship, and technical reinforcement skills while providing an employment record — directly addressing the zero-experience gap. Pay is modest but the fit is logical.
